events.title: Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake Premieres
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Russian composer's first full-length ballet score premiered at a grand theatre in the Russian capital, paired with choreography that was widely thought incompetent and dancing that was widely thought under-rehearsed. Critics focused their complaints on the music, which they found too "symphonic" for dancing. Only after the composer's death, in a restaged 1895 version with new choreography, did the ballet become a classic.
events.revealBlurb: March 4, 1877 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake at the Bolshoi, Moscow (Old Style February 20). The 1895 St. Petersburg revival with Petipa/Ivanov choreography is the version most companies perform today. The tragic black-swan finale was a 1950s restoration.

events.title: Dylan Goes Electric
events.blurb: A 24-year-old folk singer, backed by a ragged rhythm section from the previous night's acquaintance, walked onto the stage of a folk festival on a Rhode Island pier with a sunburst Stratocaster slung low over his shoulder. He played three short electric songs before some boos drowned out the applause. He walked off, returned with his acoustic, and played two more. The event marked, depending on who tells it, the birth of folk-rock or the betrayal of American folk.
events.revealBlurb: July 25, 1965 — Bob Dylan at the Newport Folk Festival. Pete Seeger, legend says, tried to cut the sound cables with an axe. Seeger later denied it. The songs included "Maggie's Farm" and "Like a Rolling Stone." Dylan's next tour was booed nightly for a year.

events.title: Monterey Pop Festival
events.blurb: A three-day rock festival on a California coastal fairground — the first major rock festival of the decade and the template for what came later — introduced American audiences to a left-handed guitarist recently returned from London, a young Otis Redding, and Janis Joplin. The left-hander, during his set, laid his guitar on the stage, knelt over it, and set it on fire with lighter fluid. The audience had not imagined such a thing was possible.
events.revealBlurb: June 16-18, 1967 — the guitarist was Jimi Hendrix, on the closing Sunday. Monterey Pop Festival drew 200,000 people. The Mamas & the Papas had organized it; proceeds went to charity. Paul McCartney recommended Hendrix and The Who to the organizers.

events.title: Woodstock Festival
events.blurb: A three-day music festival, overcapacity within hours of opening, drew an estimated 400,000 young people to a dairy farm in upstate New York despite severe rain. Fences collapsed; the event became de facto free. 32 acts performed — Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, The Who, Santana, Creedence Clearwater Revival, Joan Baez. Two people died (one from an overdose, one crushed by a tractor); two babies were born. The festival became the defining symbol of the 1960s counterculture.
events.revealBlurb: August 15-18, 1969 — on Max Yasgur's farm in Bethel, NY. Hendrix closed at 9 AM Monday morning to a dwindling crowd with a distorted, feedback-laced "Star-Spangled Banner." The 1970 documentary won an Oscar.

events.title: Dark Side of the Moon Released
events.blurb: An English progressive rock band released a conceptual album about madness, mortality, capitalism, and the passage of time, tracks flowing into each other via tape loops of spoken voices, heartbeats, and cash registers. The cover was a simple black triangular prism refracting white light into a rainbow. The album would stay on the Billboard 200 for 741 consecutive weeks — more than 14 years — a record that has never been approached.
events.revealBlurb: March 1, 1973 — Pink Floyd. Recorded at Abbey Road using then-new 16-track technology and Roger Waters' theatrical sensibility. The album has sold over 45 million copies. The "we don't need no education" band followed eight years later with another cultural juggernaut, The Wall.

events.title: Johnstown Flood
events.blurb: After days of heavy rain, a poorly maintained earth dam built to create a private lake for a Pennsylvania hunting club gave way, releasing 20 million tons of water onto the steel-mill town 23 kilometres downstream. The wall of water reached speeds of 65 km/h and was 18 metres high. It killed 2,209 people in 10 minutes.
events.revealBlurb: May 31, 1889 — Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The hunting club's members (including Andrew Carnegie and Henry Clay Frick) were never successfully sued. The flood launched the American Red Cross onto the national stage; Clara Barton ran relief operations for five months.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the western coast of Sumatra — the third-largest ever recorded — displaced so much water that tsunami waves up to 30 metres high raced across the Indian Ocean, hitting 14 countries within hours. Around 228,000 people died in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand, and as far away as Somalia. No warning system existed.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 2004 — Boxing Day. A 10-year-old British girl named Tilly Smith recognized the receding tide from a school geography lesson and got her family's Phuket beach evacuated, saving around 100 lives. A basin-wide warning system was operational by 2006.

events.title: Eyjafjallajökull Eruption
events.blurb: A glacier-capped volcano in Iceland erupted, sending a plume of fine silicate ash into the jet stream. Authorities across Europe, uncertain about engine safety, grounded all commercial aviation for six days. Around 10 million passengers were stranded, and global airlines lost an estimated $1.7 billion. Few people died, but the event showed how fragile modern mobility had become.
events.revealBlurb: April 14-20, 2010 — Iceland. The volcano's name became a running joke for newscasters. Stranded travelers included heads of state on their way to a funeral in Poland; many drove for days to get home. Rental car companies had their biggest week ever.

events.title: Maui Wildfires
events.blurb: High winds from a distant hurricane drove grass fires through a historic town on a Hawaiian island, reaching speeds that outpaced emergency alerts. 102 people died — many trapped in cars attempting to flee along a single coastal road — in the deadliest US wildfire in over a century. The 19th-century whaling-era town of Lāhainā, once the kingdom capital, was almost completely destroyed.
events.revealBlurb: August 8, 2023 — Lāhainā, Maui. The outdoor warning siren network, the largest in the world, was never activated. Some survivors escaped by jumping into the Pacific Ocean and treading water for hours. Downed Hawaiian Electric lines were identified as the likely ignition source.

events.title: Spinning Jenny Invented
events.blurb: A Lancashire weaver, semi-literate and working out of his home, built a hand-cranked multi-spindle spinning frame that let one operator spin eight threads simultaneously rather than one. Later versions spun up to 120 spindles at once. Other weavers' wives in the district, seeing their cottage-industry spinning work disappearing, broke into his house and smashed his prototypes. He patented the invention six years later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1764 — James Hargreaves in Blackburn, England. Patented 1770. The name "Jenny" is probably derived from "gin," a contemporary term for a mechanical engine — not, contrary to popular story, after his daughter. Hargreaves died in poverty in 1778.

events.title: Stockton & Darlington Railway Opens
events.blurb: A steam locomotive hauling 21 coal wagons and one passenger coach completed a 40-kilometre journey through County Durham at a top speed of 24 km/h, carrying 450 passengers on its inaugural run. It was the first railway to carry both freight and fare-paying passengers using steam traction.

events.title: Drake Strikes Oil
events.blurb: A former railroad conductor, working on behalf of a small Pennsylvania oil-extraction company, struck oil at a depth of 21 metres while drilling a well using salt-drilling techniques borrowed from Chinese craftsmen. The well produced about 25 barrels a day — at the time, world-altering. Within two years, western Pennsylvania had hundreds of wells; within twenty, American oil companies were exporting kerosene around the world; within fifty, petroleum had overtaken coal as the premier industrial fuel.
events.revealBlurb: August 27, 1859 — Edwin Drake at Titusville, Pennsylvania. Drake himself died poor; he had failed to patent his drilling-pipe innovations. John D. Rockefeller entered the Cleveland refining business five years later and, with Standard Oil, came to dominate the industry within a decade.

events.title: Bell Patents Telephone
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Scottish-born American inventor was granted a patent on "the method of, and apparatus for, transmitting vocal or other sounds telegraphically." Three days later he made the first recognized telephone call in his Boston laboratory, summoning his assistant from the next room. The patent, filed the same morning as a rival inventor's competing application, would become the most valuable patent ever issued by the US government.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1876 — Alexander Graham Bell. The first call: "Mr. Watson — come here — I want to see you." The rival, Elisha Gray, filed his caveat a few hours later; legal battles continued for years. American Telephone & Telegraph, founded on Bell's patent, became the largest corporation in the world.

events.title: Wright Brothers' First Flight
events.blurb: Two American bicycle-shop owners from Dayton, Ohio achieved the first sustained, controlled, powered flight of a heavier-than-air aircraft on a windswept dune at the Outer Banks of North Carolina. The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered 36 metres — about the wingspan of a modern commercial airliner. They made three more flights that morning; the fourth covered 260 metres in 59 seconds. Few newspapers reported the achievement; commercial aviation took another three decades to arrive.
events.revealBlurb: December 17, 1903 — Orville and Wilbur Wright at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk, NC. The flyer is now in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. The pair spent 4 years after their first flight battling patent disputes and litigation rather than manufacturing planes.

events.title: Mount Tambora Eruption
events.blurb: A volcano on an Indonesian island blew its top in the most powerful eruption in recorded history, spewing 150 cubic kilometres of material into the atmosphere. The sulphate aerosols lingered in the stratosphere for years, cooling global temperatures by roughly a degree and producing crop failures, famine, and snow in June across the northern hemisphere the following year.
events.revealBlurb: April 10, 1815 — Mount Tambora on Sumbawa, Indonesia. 1816 became "the year without a summer." Mary Shelley, trapped indoors by endless rain in Switzerland, wrote Frankenstein. J.M.W. Turner's lurid sunsets from the decade owe their color to Tambora's dust.

events.title: San Francisco Earthquake
events.blurb: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake ripped a 477-kilometre tear through the fault running up the California coast, hitting a West Coast boom city just after 5 AM. The shaking was severe, but the four-day fire that followed — fed by broken gas mains and fought with limited water from shattered pipes — did most of the damage, destroying 80 percent of the city and killing around 3,000.
events.revealBlurb: April 18, 1906 — San Francisco. The mayor authorized dynamiting buildings to create firebreaks; most of the dynamiting actually spread the fire. The opera singer Enrico Caruso, in town for a performance, vowed never to return. He didn't.

events.title: Hurricane Andrew
events.blurb: A compact Category 5 hurricane made landfall in southern Florida in the early hours of a late summer morning, its eyewall gusts reaching 280 km/h. It destroyed 63,500 houses, left 175,000 people homeless, and caused $27 billion in damage — then the costliest natural disaster in US history. Building codes across the Florida peninsula were rewritten as a direct consequence.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 1992 — Homestead, Florida. It was the first named storm of an otherwise quiet season. Eleven insurance companies went bankrupt settling claims. For comparison, Katrina 13 years later cost over $100 billion.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Iron Curtain Speech
events.blurb: A former British prime minister, speaking at a small college in Missouri at the invitation of the sitting U.S. president, declared that an impenetrable barrier had descended across the European continent from the Baltic to the Adriatic. The phrase he coined to describe it entered geopolitical vocabulary within hours.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1946 — Winston Churchill at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri. Truman sat on stage behind him. The 5,000-word speech was titled "The Sinews of Peace," but nobody remembers that part.

events.title: Stalin Dies
events.blurb: Found unconscious on the floor of his dacha outside Moscow after a late-night dinner with colleagues, a dictator who had ruled for nearly three decades lingered for four days before dying of a brain hemorrhage. His inner circle, terrified of waking him, had delayed calling doctors for many hours. His state funeral drew crowds so large that dozens were trampled.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1953 — Joseph Stalin, 74, at his Kuntsevo dacha. He'd spent the previous evening screening American westerns. His death unleashed a succession struggle; Khrushchev prevailed and began the cautious thaw.

events.title: Hungarian Revolution
events.blurb: A student demonstration in Budapest grew within hours into a nationwide uprising against a Moscow-backed government. For twelve days, a reform-minded premier announced democratic elections and withdrawal from the eastern bloc military alliance. Then 2,500 Soviet tanks rolled into the country, crushing the revolt and killing some 2,500 Hungarians.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 to November 10, 1956 — reform premier Imre Nagy was tricked into a "negotiation," arrested, and secretly executed two years later. 200,000 Hungarians fled west. The West's failure to intervene exposed the limits of containment.

events.title: Suez Crisis
events.blurb: Britain, France, and Israel invaded Egypt to seize the nationalized waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The military operation succeeded; the political one did not. Under combined U.S. and Soviet pressure, the invaders withdrew within two months. The affair is remembered as the moment Britain stopped being a great power.
events.revealBlurb: October 29 to November 7, 1956 — Eisenhower was furious he hadn't been consulted and threatened to sell US holdings of British sterling. British PM Anthony Eden resigned in disgrace three months later. Nasser emerged as the hero of the Arab world.

events.title: Chernobyl Disaster
events.blurb: During a safety test at the No. 4 reactor of a Ukrainian nuclear power plant, a power surge, flawed reactor design, and operator errors combined to blow the 1,000-tonne reactor lid off the building and send a radioactive plume across Europe. Swedish sensors detected the contamination before Moscow admitted anything had happened. The exclusion zone around the plant remains largely uninhabited nearly forty years on.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1986 — 1:23 AM. Two workers died in the initial explosion; 28 firefighters and operators died of acute radiation poisoning in the months after. Roughly 350,000 people were permanently evacuated. Cleanup cost the USSR an estimated 18 billion rubles.

events.title: Blood Circulation Described
events.blurb: An English physician published experimental evidence that blood circulates continuously through the body, pumped by the heart in a closed loop — directly contradicting the dominant view held for 1,400 years that blood was produced in the liver, consumed by the body, and never returned. He calculated that the heart beats too often and ejects too much blood per beat for any production-and-consumption model to work.
events.revealBlurb: 1628 — William Harvey's De Motu Cordis was 72 pages long and took him over a decade of dissections to verify. His contemporaries largely refused to believe him. He lost many of his patients after publication. One thing he could not explain was how blood got from arteries to veins — capillaries were too small to see with his instruments; Malpighi found them four years after Harvey's death.

events.title: On the Origin of Species Published
events.blurb: A 502-page book argued that all species of life descended from common ancestors through a process of natural selection, where individuals with heritable traits better suited to their environment survived and reproduced at higher rates. The first print run of 1,250 copies sold out to booksellers on the day it was offered for sale.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1859 — Darwin had sat on the theory for twenty years, terrified of the controversy. He finally rushed it to press only after Alfred Russel Wallace independently wrote him a letter describing the same mechanism. The two men's papers were presented jointly to the Linnean Society in 1858.

events.title: Periodic Table of Elements Published
events.blurb: A Russian chemist arranged the sixty-three known elements into a table ordered by atomic weight, discovering that chemical properties recurred in a regular pattern. He boldly left gaps for elements he predicted did not yet exist, specifying their likely weights and properties in advance — predictions that proved startlingly accurate when the missing elements were found over the following two decades.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1869 — Dmitri Mendeleev reportedly saw the complete arrangement in a dream and woke to write it down, though historians treat this story sceptically. He sent a one-page summary to chemists across Europe before the formal presentation. Germanium, gallium, and scandium were discovered later, matching his predictions closely.

events.title: Neutron Discovered
events.blurb: A British physicist bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a neutral radiation that could knock protons out of paraffin wax with remarkable force. Reasoning that gamma rays lacked the energy for such collisions, he concluded the radiation must consist of uncharged particles with roughly the mass of a proton — completing the basic structure of the atomic nucleus.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1932 — James Chadwick completed the decisive experiments in under two weeks. He mailed a letter to Nature titled "Possible Existence of a Neutron." Frédéric and Irène Joliot-Curie had the same data a month earlier but misidentified what they had found. Chadwick won the Nobel Prize in 1935.

events.title: Human Genome Project Completed
events.blurb: An international consortium announced the completion of a map of the entire 3-billion-letter chemical sequence of human DNA, covering 99 percent of gene-containing regions at 99.99 percent accuracy — two years ahead of schedule. The project, begun in 1990, required coordinating laboratories across six countries and produced a reference sequence that has underpinned virtually every major advance in genetic medicine since.
events.revealBlurb: April 14, 2003 — a rival private effort by Celera Genomics, led by Craig Venter, raced the public consortium and forced both teams to declare a joint "completion" in 2000. The actual finished sequence was only completed in 2003. A truly gapless human genome wasn't assembled until 2022, when long-read sequencing technology filled the remaining 8%.

events.title: Plessy v. Ferguson
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-1 that a Louisiana law requiring "equal but separate" railroad cars for white and Black passengers did not violate the Constitution. The decision invented the "separate but equal" doctrine that underpinned legal segregation for 58 years. Justice John Marshall Harlan's lone dissent declared the Constitution "color-blind" — a minority view for half a century.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1896. The plaintiff, Homer Plessy, was 7/8 white; he deliberately boarded a whites-only car to test the law. Harlan, a former slaveholder from Kentucky, wrote the dissent the movement would eventually vindicate.

events.title: SNCC Founded
events.blurb: At a North Carolina conference convened by a veteran activist, 200 student sit-in leaders from across the South formed a new grassroots organization to coordinate direct-action campaigns independently of older civil rights groups. The students were younger, more confrontational, and willing to risk their lives; many became the foot soldiers of the Freedom Rides, Freedom Summer, and Selma.
events.revealBlurb: April 17, 1960 — Raleigh, NC. Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, commonly pronounced "snick." Organizer Ella Baker convinced the students to stay independent rather than fold into Martin Luther King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Stokely Carmichael led it during the "Black Power" turn in 1966.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: Black Panther Party Founded
events.blurb: Two community-college students in a California Bay Area city drafted a ten-point program demanding full employment, decent housing, exemption from military service, and an end to police brutality for Black Americans. They organized armed neighborhood patrols to monitor police, opened free-breakfast programs for children, and ran medical clinics. The FBI declared them "the greatest threat to internal security" within four years.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 1966 — Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland. J. Edgar Hoover's COINTELPRO infiltrated the party and fabricated rivalries between it and the US Organization; the free breakfasts, which he called "the greatest threat," fed 20,000 children a day at their peak.

events.title: Martin Luther King Jr. Assassinated
events.blurb: Stepping onto the balcony outside Room 306 of a Tennessee motel where he was staying while supporting a sanitation workers' strike, the country's most prominent civil rights leader was shot once with a high-powered rifle from across the street. He died an hour later at a nearby hospital. He was 39. Riots broke out in more than 100 American cities within hours of the news.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1968 — Lorraine Motel, Memphis. His killer, escaped convict James Earl Ray, was captured in London two months later. The night before, King had ended a speech with: "I've been to the mountaintop. I may not get there with you, but we, as a people, will get to the Promised Land."

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
events.blurb: Walt Disney's first full-length animated feature premiered at a Los Angeles theatre — a project industry insiders had dismissed throughout its three-year production as "Disney's folly" that would bankrupt the studio. 800 artists had drawn 250,000 individual cel frames. The 83-minute film made nearly $8 million in its first release on a budget of $1.5 million, rescued the studio's finances, and launched the modern feature-animation industry.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1937 — Carthay Circle Theatre, Los Angeles. Disney received an honorary Oscar consisting of one regular-sized statuette and seven miniature ones, presented by Shirley Temple. Adjusted for inflation, the film is still among the top-grossing of all time.

events.title: The Godfather Released
events.blurb: A 32-year-old American director of partial Italian descent, working on his third feature, released a 175-minute adaptation of a recent mass-market novel about an Italian-American crime family. His studio had imposed cast, budget, and length conditions throughout production; it had also tried to fire him multiple times. The film grossed more than any previous picture in history, won Best Picture, and launched decades of imitators that have never quite matched it.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1972 — Francis Ford Coppola. Marlon Brando's sagging jowls were created with dental plumpers; Al Pacino's casting was fought bitterly by Paramount executives who wanted Ryan O'Neal. The horse's head was real — acquired from a dog-food plant.

events.title: Expulsion of the Last King of Rome
events.blurb: Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, Rome's seventh and final king, was driven into exile after his son Sextus raped the noblewoman Lucretia, who then killed herself and thereby ignited a patrician revolt led by Lucius Junius Brutus. The Romans abolished the monarchy and replaced it with two annually elected consuls — an office designed so no single man could ever hold the power of a king again.
events.revealBlurb: September 509 BCE, traditional. Lucius Junius Brutus had spent years pretending to be an imbecile — "Brutus" literally means "dullard" in Latin — to avoid being killed by the king he was plotting to overthrow.

events.title: Publication of the Twelve Tables
events.blurb: A commission of ten patricians spent two years drafting Rome's first written legal code onto twelve bronze tablets displayed in the Forum, covering debt, inheritance, property rights, and family law. The code was a concession to plebeian demands that laws stop being secret knowledge monopolised by priestly and aristocratic insiders.
events.revealBlurb: 450 BCE, Rome. Every Roman schoolboy was required to memorise the Twelve Tables for generations afterward. One clause specified that a debtor who couldn't pay could be cut into pieces by his creditors — though historians debate whether this was ever actually carried out.

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: Licinian-Sextian Laws
events.blurb: After a decade of plebeian obstruction that left Rome with no consuls at all, the tribunes Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus forced through three laws: one relieving debt, one limiting landholding to 500 iugera, and one requiring that at least one consul each year be a plebeian. Lucius Sextius duly became the first plebeian consul in 366 BCE.
events.revealBlurb: 367 BCE, Rome. Licinius and Sextius blocked every other piece of legislation for ten straight years to force the patricians to negotiate — essentially inventing the political hostage tactic of governmental gridlock.

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: Dot-com Crash
events.blurb: The NASDAQ Composite index, which had quintupled in five years on the back of unprofitable but enthusiastic internet stocks, peaked at 5,048 on a Friday morning and began a two-and-a-half-year decline that would erase nearly 78 percent of its value. Companies founded on the premise of "eyeballs" rather than revenue disappeared within months; venture capital dried up; several hundred thousand tech workers lost their jobs.
events.revealBlurb: March 10, 2000 — the NASDAQ peak. It would not regain that level until April 2015. Pets.com became the poster child of dot-com excess, burning through $300 million in 18 months to sell pet food online at a loss.

events.title: Cambridge Analytica Scandal
events.blurb: A former employee of a small British political consultancy went public with allegations that the firm had harvested personal data from some 87 million Facebook users, mostly without their knowledge or consent, and used it to build psychographic voter-targeting models for the 2016 U.S. presidential and UK Brexit campaigns. Facebook's stock lost $100 billion in market value in ten days. Its CEO was subsequently hauled before the U.S. Congress and the European Parliament.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 2018 — whistleblower Christopher Wylie in The Observer and New York Times. Cambridge Analytica went bankrupt within two months. Facebook was later fined $5 billion by the U.S. FTC — the largest fine ever for a privacy violation, but about a month's profit for the company.

events.title: TikTok Launches Globally
events.blurb: A Chinese short-video company merged its existing lip-sync-focused app Musical.ly, acquired the previous year, into a new global brand — effectively introducing mainland China's most popular short-video format to Western audiences. The app's algorithm would prove uniquely good at inferring what content users wanted without asking them. Within three years, TikTok had over a billion users and had reshaped every other social platform's product roadmap.
events.revealBlurb: August 2, 2018 — ByteDance merges Musical.ly into TikTok. By 2020, U.S. users were spending more time per day in TikTok than in Instagram or Facebook. President Trump attempted to ban it in 2020; the Biden administration attempted to force a U.S. divestment in 2024.

events.title: ChatGPT Launched
events.blurb: A San Francisco AI research lab released, as an unassuming "research preview," a conversational interface to its large language model. The chatbot could answer questions, write essays, debug code, and generate poetry in response to natural-language prompts. It gained a hundred million monthly users within two months — making it the fastest-growing consumer product in history. Incumbent tech giants pivoted their entire product strategies within weeks.
events.revealBlurb: November 30, 2022 — OpenAI. The underlying model, GPT-3.5, had existed for months; the chat wrapper made all the difference. By 2025, generative AI had become a ~$200 billion global industry. Anthropic, Google, Meta, and xAI joined OpenAI as frontier labs.

events.title: Truman Doctrine
events.blurb: Addressing a joint session of Congress, a U.S. president requested $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey and announced a sweeping new foreign policy: the United States would support "free peoples" resisting armed minorities or outside pressures. The speech committed America to global containment of communism.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1947 — Harry Truman needed just 18 minutes. Behind the rhetoric: Britain, bankrupted by war, had quietly told Washington it could no longer prop up the Greek government. America stepped into the imperial vacuum.

events.title: First Soviet Atomic Bomb Test
events.blurb: Four years after U.S. weapons ended the Pacific war, Soviet scientists detonated their own plutonium implosion device at a test range in the Kazakh steppe. Western intelligence had predicted the breakthrough was at least five years away. The explosion ended the American nuclear monopoly and opened the arms race.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 1949 — codename RDS-1, nicknamed "First Lightning." The design was largely cribbed from the U.S. Fat Man bomb via spy networks inside the Manhattan Project. Klaus Fuchs had handed over detailed blueprints.

events.title: Gorbachev Becomes Soviet Leader
events.blurb: After three elderly Soviet leaders died in rapid succession, a 54-year-old party functionary with a law degree and a distinctive birthmark on his forehead was elected General Secretary. Within months he was speaking publicly about "glasnost" (openness) and "perestroika" (restructuring). His colleagues had picked him hoping for energetic continuity. They got revolution.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1985 — Mikhail Gorbachev, the youngest Politburo member. Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko, who nominated him, said: "Comrades, this man has a nice smile, but he has iron teeth." Gorbachev won the Nobel Peace Prize five years later.

events.title: Reykjavik Summit
events.blurb: Meeting for two days in a small wooden house in the Icelandic capital, the American and Soviet leaders came astonishingly close to agreeing to eliminate all nuclear weapons within ten years. The talks collapsed over missile defense, and the two men parted grim-faced. But the intellectual groundwork had been laid for an arms-reduction treaty a year later.
events.revealBlurb: October 11-12, 1986 — Reagan and Gorbachev at Höfði House. The property was reputedly haunted. When talks broke down, Gorbachev said privately: "Can you think of any better way out?" Reagan couldn't, and walked to his car.

events.title: Tiananmen Square Protests
events.blurb: For seven weeks, student demonstrators occupied the vast plaza at the heart of the Chinese capital, demanding democratic reforms, press freedom, and an end to official corruption. Their ranks swelled into the hundreds of thousands. Then the government declared martial law, rolled tanks into the city, and cleared the square overnight, killing hundreds or thousands of civilians in the streets around it.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1989 — the crackdown. The iconic image of a lone man stopping a column of tanks was taken on June 5 from a hotel balcony. His identity remains unknown. The topic is still heavily censored inside China.

events.title: Bombay Talkies Founded
events.blurb: A studio established in Malad, Bombay, by a London-trained filmmaker and his aristocratic actress-wife drew European technical talent — German cameramen, British equipment — to build India's first modern film facility with synchronised sound stages and a Western-style star system. It launched the careers of Dilip Kumar, Ashok Kumar, and Madhubala within its first fifteen years.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1934 — founded by Himanshu Rai and Devika Rani. Rai died in 1940 while the studio was mid-production; Devika Rani, then 32, took sole control and ran it for another nine years. The studio was where a young Dilip Kumar walked in looking for work and was handed a contract he barely understood.

events.title: Mother India Released
events.blurb: A near-three-hour epic about a village woman who spends decades breaking stones, raising sons, and protecting her community from a money-lender opened on Diwali across India and broke every box-office record to that point. The following year it became India's first film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — losing by a single vote to a Federico Fellini picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1957. Directed by Mehboob Khan. Nargis, who plays the mother, married co-star Sunil Dutt after he dragged her unconscious from a fire that broke out on set. Khan's production logo featured a hammer-and-sickle; it was quietly removed before the Oscar submission print.

events.title: Anand Released
events.blurb: A terminally ill man facing lymphosarcoma of the intestine spends his remaining months arguing that life is worth celebrating — while his doctor-friend records him in a notebook — in a film whose two leads delivered career-defining performances on opposite emotional registers. Its final line, spoken after death, became among the most quoted in Hindi cinema.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1971 — directed by Hrishikesh Mukherjee, dialogues by Gulzar. Rajesh Khanna was at the absolute peak of his popularity; Amitabh Bachchan was still a supporting player. The film reportedly made Amitabh Bachchan weep on set during the final sequence — which Mukherjee kept in the film.

events.title: Deewaar Released
events.blurb: A story of two brothers who grow up in identical poverty but choose radically different paths — one becomes a dock smuggler, the other a policeman — gave Indian cinema one of its defining confrontation scenes. Its dialogue was so tightly constructed that screenwriters Salim-Javed became as famous as directors, the first time a writing duo achieved superstar status in Bollywood.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1975 — directed by Yash Chopra. Amitabh Bachchan's character has "mere paas maa hai" spoken against him, not by him — the misattribution became India's most-repeated film misquote. Director's first choices were Dev Anand and Rajesh Khanna; both were unavailable.

events.title: "Naatu Naatu" Wins Academy Award
events.blurb: A Telugu period action film about two real freedom fighters reimagined as friends on opposite sides of a colonial conflict produced a seven-minute dance sequence that, when performed live at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, brought an Oscars audience to its feet. The song became the first from an Indian film to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 2023 — the 95th Academy Awards. Composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose won. Director S.S. Rajamouli's RRR had not been submitted as India's official Oscar entry — it qualified independently through its US distributor. Singers Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava performed barefoot on the Oscars stage.

events.title: Scopes "Monkey Trial" Begins
events.blurb: John T. Scopes, a high school teacher in Dayton, Tennessee, went on trial for violating a state law banning the teaching of human evolution in public schools. The case — which pitted famed defense attorney Clarence Darrow against three-time presidential nominee and Christian fundamentalist William Jennings Bryan — was broadcast nationally on radio and drew journalists from across the country to the small town.
events.revealBlurb: July 10, 1925 — Dayton, Tennessee. The trial was deliberately staged by the town's businessmen to attract tourists and publicity; Scopes wasn't sure he had actually taught evolution. He was convicted and fined $100, but the verdict was overturned on a technicality. Bryan died five days after the trial ended.

events.title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
events.blurb: At 7:55 that morning, 353 Imperial Japanese aircraft struck the U.S. naval base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, sinking or damaging 19 ships including eight battleships and destroying 188 aircraft in under two hours. The attack killed 2,403 Americans — including 1,177 sailors and Marines aboard the USS Arizona, which exploded catastrophically and sank in nine minutes.
events.revealBlurb: December 7, 1941 — Pearl Harbor, Oahu. The USS Arizona still lies on the harbor floor; approximately 900 of her crew remain entombed inside. The declaration of war passed Congress the next day, 470–1 — the single dissenting vote was from pacifist Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana.

events.title: U.S. Invades Iraq
events.blurb: A U.S.-led coalition launched air strikes and a ground invasion of Iraq in a "shock and awe" campaign code-named Operation Iraqi Freedom, premised on intelligence assessments — later found to be wrong — that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. The initial combat phase lasted 41 days; the subsequent occupation and insurgency lasted until 2011 and killed more than 4,400 American service members.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 2003 — Baghdad, Iraq. No weapons of mass destruction were found. Saddam Hussein was captured hiding in a hole near Tikrit in December 2003 and executed by hanging in December 2006. President Bush declared "Mission Accomplished" on May 1, 2003, from the deck of an aircraft carrier; the war continued for eight more years.

events.title: Lehman Brothers Collapses: 2008 Financial Crisis
events.blurb: Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy — the largest bankruptcy in American history, with over $600 billion in assets — triggering a global financial panic that erased more than $10 trillion in U.S. household wealth and produced the worst economic downturn since the 1930s. The failure stemmed from the firm's enormous exposure to mortgage-backed securities tied to a collapsing housing market.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 2008 — New York City. The Federal Reserve and Treasury had just rescued Bear Stearns and Fannie Mae but declined to backstop Lehman. The Dow dropped 504 points that day — and lost another 33% over the next three months. TARP, a $700 billion bank rescue program, was signed into law 19 days later.

events.title: COVID-19 National Emergency Declared
events.blurb: President Donald Trump declared a national emergency, unlocking $50 billion in federal disaster funds to respond to the coronavirus pandemic, which had by then spread to 49 states and killed dozens of Americans. The pandemic would ultimately claim over 1.1 million American lives — more than any war in the country's history — and shut down schools, businesses, and public life for over a year.
events.revealBlurb: March 13, 2020 — The White House. The first confirmed U.S. case had been detected just 53 days earlier. Within weeks, American unemployment reached 14.7% — the highest since the Great Depression — as roughly 22 million jobs vanished in two months.

events.title: Botticelli's Primavera
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a large poplar panel for the bedroom of a Medici cousin, depicting nine mythological figures in a grove of orange trees — Venus at the centre, the Three Graces dancing, a gusting wind god chasing a nymph who is transformed into the flower-bearing goddess of spring. It is among the first Renaissance paintings to take mythological (not religious) subject matter on its own terms.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1482 — Sandro Botticelli. The painting contains at least 500 identifiable plant species, some 190 different flowers. Botticelli was later nearly destroyed by Savonarola's movement and reportedly burned some of his own work in the bonfire of the vanities.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Armory Show Opens
events.blurb: An exhibition at a New York National Guard armory introduced American audiences to European modernism at industrial scale — 1,300 paintings and sculptures by artists most had never heard of, including Matisse, Picasso, Duchamp, and Brancusi. Duchamp's "Nude Descending a Staircase No. 2" was ridiculed by a popular cartoonist as "explosion in a shingle factory" and drew crowds for exactly that reason. The show moved on to Chicago and Boston and is credited with changing the course of American art.
events.revealBlurb: February 17 to March 15, 1913 — the 69th Regiment Armory, Lexington Avenue, NYC. Around 90,000 people visited in New York alone. Theodore Roosevelt wrote a mostly-baffled review; a reproduction of the "Nude" was burned in effigy at the Chicago Art Institute.

events.title: Dalí's Persistence of Memory
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Spanish surrealist painted a small oil on canvas — only 24 by 33 cm — showing four pocket watches, one covered in ants, draped limply over a tree branch, a bier, and a distorted horse-headed figure in a landscape of Catalan coast. He said the idea came from contemplating a runny camembert cheese. The ants, the soft watches, and the empty landscape have become visual shorthand for dreamlike unreality.
events.revealBlurb: 1931 — Salvador Dalí. Now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Dalí painted a second version, "The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory," 23 years later. He is said to have visualized in reverse: imagining the picture whole and then painting what he saw.

events.title: Pollock's Drip Paintings
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American painter, working in a converted barn studio on Long Island, laid large unstretched canvases on the floor and moved around their edges pouring and flinging paint from sticks and hardened brushes. The resulting "drip paintings" rejected representational composition entirely in favour of overall visual rhythm. A 1949 Life magazine spread asked: "Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?" and made him instantly famous and nearly famously alcoholic.
events.revealBlurb: 1947 — Jackson Pollock began the drip technique in Springs, NY. He died in a car crash driving drunk on August 11, 1956, aged 44. His "No. 5, 1948" sold privately in 2006 for $140 million, briefly the highest price ever paid for a painting.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: World Wide Web Proposed
events.blurb: A British software engineer working at a Swiss particle-physics laboratory circulated an internal memo proposing a distributed hypertext information management system that would link documents across different computers. His supervisor scribbled "Vague, but exciting" across the top and approved further work. The project would take two more years to become a working system.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1989 — Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. His supervisor was Mike Sendall. Berners-Lee never sought patents on his web protocols; he believed the only way they'd spread was to give them away. Queen Elizabeth II knighted him in 2004.

events.title: Intel Pentium Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the fifth generation of its mass-market microprocessor under the brand name "Pentium" — a word coined to be trademarkable, since numerical names like "586" were not. The chip included 3.1 million transistors and outperformed its 486 predecessor by a factor of two. A subtle floating-point division bug discovered by a math professor the following year forced a $475 million recall.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1993 — Intel Pentium (P5). The floating-point bug (the FDIV bug) was discovered by Thomas Nicely of Lynchburg College. Initially Intel offered replacements only to customers who could prove they used the chip for heavy math. Bad PR forced full replacement.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: First Spacewalk
events.blurb: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and spent 12 minutes and 9 seconds in open space — the first human extravehicular activity. His spacesuit then ballooned in the vacuum to the point where he could no longer fit back through the hatch, forcing him to bleed pressure from a valve before squeezing inside headfirst.
events.revealBlurb: March 18, 1965 — Voskhod 2. The suit's engineers had fitted it with a built-in suicide pill. Leonov later said sweat filled his boots to the knee from the exertion of forcing himself back in. The spacecraft also drifted into an unplanned orbit and landed 386 km off target in the Ural mountains, where the crew spent a night in wolf country.

events.title: ISS First Crewed Occupation
events.blurb: A three-person crew docked a Soyuz capsule to the International Space Station's Zvezda module at 09:21 UTC, beginning a continuous human presence in low Earth orbit that has not been interrupted since. The station at that point consisted of three connected modules spanning roughly 27 meters, a fraction of its eventual 109-meter length.
events.revealBlurb: November 2, 2000 — Expedition 1. Commander Bill Shepherd radioed NASA to request the station's call sign be changed from "Alpha" to "International Space Station" — a small act of diplomacy that stuck. The crew of two Russians and one American had access to less than 425 cubic meters of living space, about the volume of a large school bus.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Cassini Enters Saturn Orbit
events.blurb: The Cassini–Huygens spacecraft fired its main engine for 96 minutes to decelerate into Saturn orbit, threading a gap between the planet's F and G rings — a maneuver so precisely executed that the trajectory team reported it arrived within one kilometer of the planned position. Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, beginning a 13-year study of the planet and its moons.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 2004 — Cassini. Six months later, Cassini released the Huygens probe, which descended through Titan's atmosphere and transmitted data from its surface — the most distant landing ever achieved at the time. Cassini ultimately discovered that Enceladus has active geysers of water vapor, making it one of the top candidates for extraterrestrial life.

events.title: Perseverance Mars Rover Landing
events.blurb: NASA's Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater — a 45 km ancient river delta — using the same sky-crane system as Curiosity but upgraded with a terrain-relative navigation system that steered around boulders autonomously during descent. The mission carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which made the first powered flight on another planet six weeks after landing.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 2021 — Mars 2020. Perseverance carries 43 sealed titanium tubes designed to cache Martian rock samples for a future return mission — a plan with no confirmed launch date but an estimated $10 billion price tag. It also produced breathable oxygen from the Martian atmosphere using an instrument called MOXIE, demonstrating a technology critical for crewed Mars missions.

events.title: Founding of Rome
events.blurb: According to Roman tradition, Romulus killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel over the city's walls, then became the first king of a settlement of seven hills beside the Tiber. Varro, working backward from consular lists, calculated the exact date centuries later and Rome adopted it as its birthday, celebrating it annually with the Parilia festival.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 753 BCE — the traditional date. Romulus allegedly populated his new city by opening it as a sanctuary for fugitives, runaway slaves, and exiles. When women were in short supply, he invited the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and had his men abduct their daughters.

events.title: The Antonine Plague
events.blurb: Soldiers returning from campaigns in Parthia brought a disease — almost certainly smallpox — that spread from the eastern frontier through every province of the empire over fifteen years. The physician Galen, the most famous doctor of his age, documented symptoms in detail from Rome itself; at the plague's peak witnesses recorded 2,000 deaths per day in the capital alone.
events.revealBlurb: 165–180 CE. Galen's treatment recommendation included keeping patients warm and feeding them milk — the best care available, and completely ineffective. The plague killed co-emperor Lucius Verus in 169 CE and may have killed up to 10% of the empire's total population.

events.title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
events.blurb: The philosopher-emperor Marcus Aurelius died of illness at the Danubian frontier, most likely at Vindobona, at the age of 58 after nineteen years of near-constant warfare against Germanic tribes. He chose to pass the empire to his biological son Commodus rather than adopt a capable successor, ending the run of four successive emperors who had done exactly that.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 180 CE. Marcus kept a private notebook of philosophical reflections — the Meditations — with no apparent intention of publication. One entry reads: "Loss is nothing else but change, and change is Nature's delight." He died of the same plague he had spent a decade governing around.

events.title: Caracalla's Citizenship Edict
events.blurb: Emperor Caracalla issued a decree granting full Roman citizenship to every free person throughout the empire, erasing a 700-year distinction between citizen and non-citizen that had shaped Roman law, military service, and taxation. Modern historians debate whether the primary motive was ideological universalism or a straightforward need to expand the tax base.
events.revealBlurb: July 11, 212 CE. Caracalla's full name — Marcus Aurelius Severus Antoninus — was a collection of borrowed dynastic brands. "Caracalla" was the nickname Romans gave him, after a Gallic hooded cloak he popularised. He had his brother and co-emperor Geta killed months before signing this edict.

events.title: Diocletian's Tetrarchy
events.blurb: Recognising that one man could not govern and defend an empire stretching from Scotland to Mesopotamia, Emperor Diocletian formalised a system of four co-rulers — two senior Augusti and two junior Caesars — each commanding a quarter of the empire from a frontier capital. He also doubled the size of the army, reformed the tax system, and set maximum prices for hundreds of goods.
events.revealBlurb: 293 CE. Diocletian is the only Roman emperor to voluntarily abdicate and retire — he went to grow cabbages in his palace at Split (modern Croatia). When colleagues urged him to return, he reportedly replied that if they could see the cabbages he had grown, they would not ask.

events.title: Salt March Begins
events.blurb: A 60-year-old lawyer in a homespun loincloth set out from his ashram with 78 followers to walk 390 kilometres to the coast, intending to violate a colonial monopoly by picking up a pinch of seawater-evaporated salt. The 24-day trek grew into a procession of thousands; the defiance of the salt law spread across the country within weeks. 60,000 Indians, including the leader himself, were jailed within three months.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1930 — Gandhi begins the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram. Newspapers across the world carried photographs of him scooping up salt on the beach on April 6. Winston Churchill, watching from Westminster, privately described the prospect of "seditious middle-temple lawyer" meeting the viceroy as nauseating.

events.title: Bhagat Singh Executed
events.blurb: Three young revolutionaries were hanged an hour earlier than scheduled at a jail in a Punjabi city, after a three-year trial for killing a British police officer they had mistaken for the superintendent they had meant to assassinate. The youngest of them was 23. Crowds had gathered outside the prison expecting the normal morning execution time; by the time they arrived, the bodies had already been smuggled out and cremated by the riverside.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1931 — Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev at Lahore Central Jail. Their martyrdom made them arguably the most venerated revolutionaries of the independence movement, an icon Gandhi's non-violent path never quite matched among the young.

events.title: Gandhi Assassinated
events.blurb: A 78-year-old man, walking slowly across a Delhi lawn supported by two of his grandnieces, was shot three times in the chest at point-blank range by a Hindu nationalist who blamed him for indulging Muslims and accepting partition. He fell murmuring the name of a god. He had survived five previous attempts on his life.
events.revealBlurb: January 30, 1948 — the assassin was Nathuram Godse, a former editor of a Hindu nationalist newspaper. He was convicted and executed. Gandhi had warned his secretary that morning that his life's work would not be judged "until after I am dead and gone."

events.title: Babri Masjid Demolition
events.blurb: A mob of around 150,000 Hindu nationalists who had gathered for what was officially billed as a symbolic prayer ceremony at a disputed 16th-century mosque in a north Indian town overpowered the police cordon and demolished the structure with pickaxes and crowbars over six hours. Riots across the country in the following weeks killed 2,000 people, mostly Muslims. A Hindu temple now stands on the site, inaugurated 31 years later.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1992 — Ayodhya. The Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the demolition was illegal, but awarded the site to the Hindu temple trust. The Ram Mandir was consecrated on January 22, 2024.

events.title: Kargil War
events.blurb: Pakistani soldiers, disguised as local insurgents, occupied high-altitude ridges inside the Indian-administered portion of a disputed northern territory over the winter. Their discovery by a shepherd in early May touched off a 74-day war fought at elevations up to 5,600 metres. India retook the peaks one by one with heavy infantry losses; Pakistan, pressured by Washington, withdrew.
events.revealBlurb: May 3 to July 26, 1999 — the Line of Control in Kargil, Ladakh. The conflict was one of the first televised wars in India. Captain Vikram Batra became a national hero before dying on Point 4875 on July 7.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Hoover Dam Completed
events.blurb: A 221-metre concrete arch-gravity dam across the Colorado River at a deep canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border was completed two years ahead of schedule, creating what was at the time the largest reservoir on the planet. The dam's construction employed 16,000 workers during the worst years of the Great Depression; 96 died during the 5-year project. It generated 2,080 megawatts, ran every light in Las Vegas, irrigated a million acres, and made the Los Angeles basin's growth possible.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1935 — originally called the Boulder Dam under Roosevelt's administration; renamed 1947 after Herbert Hoover, who had championed the project as Commerce Secretary. Around 6 million tons of concrete went into it — enough, with less, to pave a two-lane road from San Francisco to New York.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Henry VIII Breaks with Rome
events.blurb: An English parliament passed an Act of Supremacy declaring the king — who had wanted for years to annul his marriage to a Spanish princess who had given him no male heir, and whom the pope had refused — the "Supreme Head" of the Church of England. The break with Rome was not primarily theological; the king remained Catholic in doctrine for the rest of his life. It rewrote England's religious, political, and property landscape for the next century.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1534 — Henry VIII. He had already married Anne Boleyn (his second wife) in secret in January 1533. The archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, had annulled his first marriage in May. Henry would have six wives; two were beheaded, two divorced, one died in childbirth.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: Dutch East India Company Founded
events.blurb: The Dutch government chartered a joint-stock corporation with a 21-year monopoly on Asian trade, the authority to wage war, build forts, coin money, and conclude treaties in the name of the States General. It was the world's first publicly traded multinational corporation. Within decades it dominated the Asian spice trade, conquered chunks of Southeast Asia, and declared its own wars. At its height its market capitalization exceeded that of the combined top ten companies of today.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 1602 — Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC). It employed over 70,000 people at its peak. Its share price rose 1,200 percent in the 1600s and collapsed in 1799 when the company was bankrupted by corruption, wars, and changing trade patterns.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Mosaic Browser Released
events.blurb: Undergraduate students at a University of Illinois supercomputing centre released a graphical web browser for Unix, with a version for Windows and Mac released later in the year. Unlike the earlier terminal-based browsers, it could display images inline with text. Within 18 months, web traffic had grown by 10,000 percent. The browser's lead developer would leave to co-found a company that would dominate the next phase.
events.revealBlurb: April 22, 1993 — developed at the NCSA, lead developer Marc Andreessen. Andreessen co-founded Netscape within a year. Mosaic was free for non-commercial use, a decision that gave the web the critical mass it needed.

events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: Y2K Rollover
events.blurb: As the world's time zones successively crossed the boundary between the 20th and 21st centuries, decades of doomsday predictions — that computer systems storing years as two digits would interpret "00" as 1900 and crash vital infrastructure — largely failed to materialize. An estimated $300 billion had been spent worldwide on remediation code. Whether the peaceful transition vindicated the expense or exposed it as overblown remains contested.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 2000 — New Zealand and Pacific islands hit midnight first, without incident. Actual bugs did occur — a French meteorological satellite briefly misreported dates, some slot machines froze, a few nuclear plants had cooling-monitor glitches — but nothing catastrophic. The fix, written in COBOL in the 1990s, may be the largest software project ever.

events.title: Twitter's First Tweet
events.blurb: A 29-year-old podcasting-company engineer tested a prototype microblogging platform the team had built in two weeks as a side project, posting the five-word message "just setting up my twttr." Users were limited to 140 characters, the carrier limit for SMS text messages, since the service was originally designed to be usable by phone text. Within four years the service would be blamed — and credited — for upending journalism, politics, and activism.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 2006 — Jack Dorsey's first tweet. Co-founders included Biz Stone, Noah Glass, and Evan Williams. Elon Musk bought the company for $44 billion in 2022 and renamed it X the following year. Dorsey's original tweet was auctioned as an NFT for $2.9 million in 2021.

events.title: Dunkirk Evacuation
events.blurb: Over nine days, 338,000 soldiers trapped against the sea by encircling armoured forces were lifted off a French beach by an improvised armada of naval destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, and private pleasure craft — while a rearguard held a tightening perimeter and aircraft fought overhead to keep the sky contested.
events.revealBlurb: May 26 – June 4, 1940 — Operation Dynamo. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; they got 338,226. The "little ships" — about 700 civilian vessels ranging from lifeboats to Thames paddle steamers — became a national legend. Churchill warned Parliament not to call it a victory: "Wars are not won by evacuations."

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Birkenau Gas Chambers Operational
events.blurb: Four large purpose-built structures combining undressing rooms, sealed chambers, and industrial crematoria were completed and put into continuous operation at a camp in occupied Poland, creating a killing capacity of several thousand people per day and establishing the industrial infrastructure used to murder the majority of the Holocaust's victims.
events.revealBlurb: The four large crematoria-gas chamber complexes at Auschwitz-Birkenau came fully operational between March and June 1943. At peak operation in the summer of 1944, during the deportation of Hungarian Jews, they killed and cremated up to 10,000 people per day. The Sonderkommando — prisoner workers forced to operate the crematoria — later buried written testimony in the ash.

events.title: Tehran Conference
