events.blurb: The three most powerful leaders of the opposing alliance met for the first time in a capital city in southwest Asia, committing to a firm timeline for a massive cross-channel invasion in spring, agreeing on the postwar borders of one eastern European nation, and beginning to sketch the political shape of the world that would follow the conflict.
events.revealBlurb: November 28 – December 1, 1943 — FDR, Churchill, and Stalin met in Tehran. It was the first time FDR and Stalin met in person. Roosevelt, whose security staff feared assassination, moved into the Soviet Embassy at Stalin's suggestion — and Soviet intelligence promptly bugged his suite. Churchill celebrated his 69th birthday at the conference with a dinner attended by all three leaders.

events.title: Nuremberg Verdicts
events.blurb: An international tribunal delivered verdicts against 22 senior leaders of a defeated regime after ten months of proceedings that introduced "crimes against humanity" as a concept in international law — finding twelve guilty of offences for which they would be executed, and establishing the principle that following government orders is not a defence against such charges.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1946. Hermann Göring cheated the hangman by swallowing a cyanide capsule hours before his scheduled execution — a capsule no one ever satisfactorily explained. The other ten were hanged on October 16. Three defendants were acquitted. The tribunal's procedural framework became the model for every subsequent international war crimes court.

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Napoleon Abdicates to Elba
events.blurb: Coalition armies having entered Paris and the French Senate having deposed him, a French emperor signed an abdication at a palace outside the capital. A subsequent treaty exiled him to a small Italian Mediterranean island, where he was permitted the title of Emperor of Elba, 400 soldiers, and an annual pension. He would escape ten months later, raise a new army in a few weeks, and rule for a final hundred days before Waterloo.
events.revealBlurb: April 6, 1814 — Fontainebleau. Napoleon's first suicide attempt, swallowing a poison he had carried since Russia, had been unsuccessful (the poison had degraded). He escaped Elba on February 26, 1815 and returned to Paris by March 20 without a shot being fired at him.

events.title: First Smallpox Vaccination
events.blurb: An English country doctor inoculated a healthy eight-year-old boy with material extracted from a milkmaid's cowpox blister, then six weeks later deliberately exposed the child to smallpox. When the boy showed no symptoms, the physician had demonstrated that a mild related disease could confer immunity against a deadly one — founding the practice of vaccination.

events.title: Koch Identifies TB Bacillus
events.blurb: A 38-year-old German physician, presenting to the Berlin Physiological Society, announced he had isolated and cultured the bacillus responsible for tuberculosis — a disease that killed roughly one in seven people in 19th-century Europe. He had developed systematic protocols — now called Koch's postulates — for identifying which microbes caused which diseases. He would identify the cholera bacillus two years later.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1882 — Robert Koch. World Tuberculosis Day is commemorated on this anniversary each year. Koch won the Nobel Prize in 1905. His attempted TB vaccine, tuberculin, was a failure — but became a useful skin test for TB exposure.

events.title: Fleming Discovers Penicillin
events.blurb: A 47-year-old Scottish bacteriologist returning from a summer holiday to his London laboratory noticed that one of the staphylococcus-culture plates he had left stacked on his bench had been contaminated by a mold, and that a clear zone of inhibition around the mold showed the bacteria had died there. He identified the mold genus, isolated an anti-bacterial substance it produced, and published his findings — which were largely ignored for over a decade.
events.revealBlurb: September 28, 1928 — Alexander Fleming at St Mary's Hospital, London. Howard Florey and Ernst Chain at Oxford successfully purified penicillin in 1941, making it a usable drug. They shared the 1945 Nobel with Fleming. The drug's mass production during WWII saved hundreds of thousands of Allied soldiers' lives.

events.title: First Heart Transplant
events.blurb: A South African surgeon led a nine-hour operation at a Cape Town hospital transplanting the heart of a 25-year-old woman, killed by a car striking her as she crossed the road to buy cake, into the chest of a 54-year-old man with severe coronary disease. The patient lived 18 days before dying of pneumonia. The surgeon instantly became internationally famous; subsequent transplant patients lived increasingly long with improved immunosuppression.
events.revealBlurb: December 3, 1967 — Christiaan Barnard at Groote Schuur Hospital, Cape Town. Patient: Louis Washkansky. Donor: Denise Darvall. Barnard's second patient, Philip Blaiberg, lived 19 months. The 5-year survival rate for heart transplants is now about 75 percent.

events.title: First COVID-19 Vaccine Authorized
events.blurb: The US Food and Drug Administration issued an emergency use authorization for a novel mRNA-based vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, developed in less than a year from the publication of the virus's genetic sequence — a timescale previously thought impossible for a vaccine. The mRNA technology, which instructs the body's own cells to produce viral spike protein that the immune system then learns to recognize, had been in development for decades but had never been used in a licensed vaccine.
events.revealBlurb: December 11, 2020 — Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Moderna's similar mRNA vaccine followed December 18. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose basic mRNA research had been neglected for years, won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Over 13 billion COVID vaccine doses were administered globally in the first three years.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Caesar Crosses the Rubicon
events.blurb: A Roman general returning from nine years of conquest in Gaul, forbidden by law from bringing his army across the small river marking the boundary of Italy proper, led a single legion across anyway — knowing the act constituted treason against the Republic. He was reportedly quoting a Greek tragedian: "the die is cast." His subsequent march on Rome ignited a four-year civil war, at the end of which he emerged as a dictator-for-life and the Republic ended in everything but name.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 49 BCE — Julius Caesar with Legion XIII. "Alea iacta est" — "the die is cast" — is attributed to him crossing. The Rubicon itself is a small, easily missable river in northern Italy; its modern identity is still debated by historians. The phrase "crossing the Rubicon" has since become an English idiom.

events.title: Diocletian Divides the Empire
events.blurb: A Roman emperor, facing multiple simultaneous military crises on widely separated frontiers and concluding that the imperial job had become too large for one man, appointed a co-emperor to rule the western half of the empire while he concentrated on the east. He later elaborated the system into a tetrarchy — two senior emperors and two junior Caesars, each with his own court and capital. The political unity of Rome was effectively over; the imperial division became permanent in 395 CE.
events.revealBlurb: 285-286 CE — Diocletian and Maximian. He established his own capital at Nicomedia (modern Izmit), not Rome — and abdicated voluntarily in 305 CE to grow cabbages at his palace in Split (modern Croatia), the only Roman emperor ever to retire. His palace still stands at the center of Split's old town.

events.title: Fall of Constantinople
events.blurb: An Ottoman sultan, 21 years old, directed a 53-day siege of the Byzantine capital with 80,000 troops, an army of miners who tunneled under the walls, and enormous bronze cannons that fired 550-kilogram stone balls. The last Roman emperor died fighting at a breach in his city's walls. The 1,100-year-old Byzantine state, the direct legal continuation of Roman rule, ended.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1453 — Mehmed II. The city's Greek name, Constantinople, stayed in formal Ottoman use until 1930; "Istanbul" is how Byzantine Greeks had always said "to the city" colloquially. Hagia Sophia became a mosque that Friday.

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Mozart's Requiem Unfinished
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Austrian composer who had been commissioned by a mysterious stranger six months earlier to compose a requiem Mass for an anonymous client died in his Vienna apartment with the work unfinished. Much of the "Dies irae" and "Lacrimosa" had been sketched only. His widow, in desperate financial circumstances, had a student complete the work to secure the remaining half of the commission fee.
events.revealBlurb: December 5, 1791 — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, aged 35. The mysterious stranger was Count Walsegg, who meant to pass the work off as his own for his late wife. Mozart's student Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed it; his contributions have been debated ever since.

events.title: Beethoven's Ninth Premieres
events.blurb: A nearly deaf 53-year-old composer, standing on the podium while a co-conductor did the actual directing, premiered a vast hour-long symphony that broke with convention by adding four vocal soloists and a chorus to the orchestra in its final movement. The text was a Schiller poem celebrating universal brotherhood. At the end the composer had to be turned around by one of the singers to see the audience — which he otherwise could not hear — thundering applause.
events.revealBlurb: May 7, 1824 — Ludwig van Beethoven at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna. He had been profoundly deaf for over a decade. The "Ode to Joy" theme is now, somewhat jarringly given the text, the official anthem of the European Union.

events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: Altamont Free Concert
events.blurb: A free Rolling Stones concert at a dusty California motor speedway, hastily organized as a West Coast Woodstock, instead became the counterculture's dark counterpart. Hells Angels motorcycle gang members had been hired to provide stage security in exchange for $500 worth of beer. Fights broke out throughout the day; during the Rolling Stones' set an Angel stabbed an 18-year-old audience member to death within a metre of the stage.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1969 — Altamont Speedway, California. The victim was Meredith Hunter, 18; the Angel who stabbed him, Alan Passaro, was acquitted on grounds of self-defense. The 1970 documentary "Gimme Shelter" captures the killing.

events.title: Hatshepsut Declares Herself Pharaoh
events.blurb: A woman who had been serving as regent for a young male heir declared herself co-ruler with full royal titles and the double crown — an act without known precedent in more than a thousand years of Egyptian kingship. She commissioned monuments at Karnak, sent a major trading expedition south to the land of Punt, and built a three-tiered mortuary temple at the base of a cliff that still stands. She ruled for roughly twenty years until her death.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1473 BCE — Thebes, Egypt. Hatshepsut, 18th Dynasty. After her death, her successor Thutmose III had her images chiseled from monuments — possibly decades later, not immediately. Egyptologists rediscovered who she was only in the 19th century after piecing together erased cartouches.

events.title: Phoenician Alphabet Comes Into Use
events.blurb: Merchants and scribes along the eastern Mediterranean coast standardized a writing system using 22 consonant letters — the first alphabet with a fixed right-to-left writing direction. The system required no specialist training to learn and could be adapted to write almost any spoken language. It spread rapidly through sea trade to Greece, where vowel letters were added, producing the ancestor of every modern European alphabet.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1050 BCE — Levantine coast (modern Lebanon). The Phoenician alphabet evolved from earlier Proto-Canaanite scripts. The oldest securely dated inscription is on a bronze arrowhead from around 1000 BCE. Within three centuries, adapted versions of this script would be writing Greek, Aramaic, Hebrew, and Arabic.

events.title: Nebuchadnezzar II Destroys the Temple in Jerusalem
events.blurb: After an 18-month siege, a Babylonian army breached the walls of a fortified hill city in the Levant, razed its palace and principal temple to the ground, and deported the ruling class, clergy, and skilled artisans to Babylon. The deportation was done en masse rather than dispersed, allowing the exiled community to maintain its cultural coherence. The destruction ended a continuous religious and political tradition that had lasted roughly four centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 586 BCE — Jerusalem (modern Israel). Nebuchadnezzar II, Neo-Babylonian Empire. The Babylonian Chronicle independently corroborates the date of the earlier 597 BCE siege. Archaeological excavations in Jerusalem have found destruction layers with burned grain, arrowheads, and Babylonian-style pottery.

events.title: Library of Alexandria Established
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's scholarly advisor was charged with assembling a universal library in the new capital city — a building intended to collect every text ever written, in every language. Ships arriving in the harbor were searched for scrolls, which were confiscated, copied, and returned. The institution was attached to a research center called the Mouseion where scholars in medicine, mathematics, astronomy, and literature received royal stipends to work full-time.
events.revealBlurb: c. 295 BCE — Alexandria, Egypt. Conceived by Ptolemy I; built under Ptolemy II. Demetrius of Phalerum, an Athenian philosopher, was the founding librarian. The library eventually held an estimated 400,000–700,000 scrolls. It did not burn in a single dramatic fire — it declined gradually over centuries.

events.title: Rosetta Stone Decree Issued
events.blurb: A congress of priests convened at Memphis to celebrate a royal coronation and issued a decree granting temple tax exemptions, priestly stipend increases, prisoner amnesty, and renewed support for sacred animal cults. The decree was engraved in two forms of Egyptian script and in Greek onto a granodiorite stele and distributed to temples across the country. The king in whose honor it was issued was thirteen years old.
events.revealBlurb: March 27, 196 BCE — Memphis, Egypt. Ptolemy V Epiphanes. The stele was later carried off by French soldiers in 1799, surrendered to the British, and now sits in the British Museum. Champollion used it in 1822 to crack Egyptian hieroglyphics.

events.title: Cartwright Patents Power Loom
events.blurb: A 42-year-old Anglican clergyman with no mechanical training, visiting a Derbyshire cotton mill, was so struck by the mismatch between fast-spinning machinery and hand weaving that he went home and built a water-powered weaving loom. His early designs barely worked, but subsequent refinements by others made mechanical weaving commercially viable by the 1820s and obsolete the ancient hand-loom trade. Hundreds of thousands of English and Indian weavers lost their livelihoods.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1785 — Edmund Cartwright. His brother had predicted that Arkwright's spinning machines would flood the market with yarn that hand-weavers could not process; the power loom was his answer. His own mill burned down twice, possibly by angered hand-weavers.

events.title: Liverpool-Manchester Railway Opens
events.blurb: The world's first inter-city passenger railway line opened with ceremony, carrying dignitaries including the Duke of Wellington on eight parallel trains along a 56-kilometre line linking the port of Liverpool with the cotton-manufacturing centre of Manchester. A parliamentary member, William Huskisson, stepped onto the tracks at a refueling stop and was struck by an oncoming locomotive. He died that evening — the first well-known railway fatality.
events.revealBlurb: September 15, 1830 — designed by George Stephenson. Huskisson is universally regarded as the first prominent casualty of the railway age, though he was not strictly the first railway death. The line ran horse- and steam-hauled freight alongside passengers for its first decades.

events.title: Transatlantic Telegraph Cable Completed
events.blurb: The steamship Great Eastern finished laying 4,000 kilometres of insulated copper wire across the floor of the Atlantic, connecting Valencia Island, Ireland, to Heart's Content, Newfoundland. The first commercial message crossed in minutes — a journey that had previously taken ten days by ship.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Ford Model T Goes on Sale
events.blurb: An American automaker released a new car designed to be cheap, simple to drive, and reliable on the rutted rural roads of the era. It sold for $850 — about half the price of the cheapest competitor. Over 19 years of production, the company would build 15 million of them, mostly painted black because that paint dried fastest. At peak production, a completed Model T rolled off the line every 24 seconds.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1908 — Ford Motor Company. The 1913-1914 introduction of the moving assembly line cut the Model T's price to $490. Henry Ford doubled the minimum wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day in January 1914, partly to cut turnover caused by the line's brutal monotony.

events.title: Lascaux Cave Paintings
events.blurb: In a limestone complex in southwestern France, Paleolithic artists over multiple generations painted some 6,000 bulls, deer, horses, and abstract signs along narrow corridors and a soaring "Hall of the Bulls" as large as a Romanesque nave. The largest painted bull is over five metres long. The cave was rediscovered in 1940 by four teenagers and their dog investigating a tree that had been uprooted by a storm.
events.revealBlurb: c. 17,000 BCE — Montignac, Dordogne. The original cave was closed to visitors in 1963 when tourist breath and carbon dioxide began damaging the pigments. Lascaux II, III, and IV — increasingly faithful replicas — have been opened to the public.

events.title: Terracotta Army Created
events.blurb: In a pit 1.5 kilometres east of the tomb of a Chinese emperor who had just died, labourers arranged some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers, 130 chariots, and 670 horses facing east, ready to defend him in the afterlife. Each soldier's face was modelled individually; no two are identical. The figures had originally been painted in bright colours that flaked off within days of excavation when exposed to dry modern air.
events.revealBlurb: c. 210 BCE — the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of unified China. Rediscovered by local farmers drilling a well in March 1974. The emperor's own tomb mound remains unexcavated — ancient sources describe rivers of mercury; soil tests confirm unusual mercury levels.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: The Last Supper Completed
events.blurb: An Italian polymath completed a 9-metre-wide mural in the refectory of a Dominican convent in a northern Italian city, depicting Christ announcing his betrayal and the instant of shocked reaction on the faces of his twelve disciples. The artist had worked on it for three years, painting in oil on a dry wall rather than true fresco — a choice that made the picture deteriorate visibly within his own lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: 1498 — Leonardo da Vinci in Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. His experimental technique began flaking within 20 years. The painting has been restored many times, most recently between 1978 and 1999. Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed the refectory roof but the wall survived.

events.title: Van Gogh Cuts Off His Ear
events.blurb: After a violent argument with a fellow painter who had been living with him at a small yellow house in Provence for nine weeks, a 35-year-old Dutch artist cut off part of his own left ear with a razor, wrapped it in newspaper, and walked through the rain to deliver the package to a woman at a nearby brothel. He spent the night lying in a pool of blood. The fellow painter left the next morning. The injured man was committed to an asylum.
events.revealBlurb: December 23, 1888 — Vincent van Gogh; the houseguest was Paul Gauguin. He painted "Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear" within weeks. He sold only one painting in his lifetime and shot himself 19 months later in a Paris suburb.

events.title: First Ancient Olympic Games
events.blurb: A religious festival held every four years in honour of Zeus at a sacred grove in the western Peloponnese began with a single footrace — a sprint of about 192 metres — won by a cook from the nearby city of Elis. Over subsequent centuries, the games expanded to include additional running events, wrestling, boxing, pankration, pentathlon, and chariot racing. The festival ran continuously for nearly 1,200 years before a Christian emperor banned it.
events.revealBlurb: 776 BCE — traditional date of first games at Olympia; winner Coroebus of Elis. The festival was abolished by Emperor Theodosius I in 393 CE as part of his suppression of pagan rites. It was revived as the modern Olympics in Athens, 1896.

events.title: First Modern Olympics
events.blurb: The first modern Summer Olympic Games opened in an Athens marble stadium built on the foundations of a Panathenaic-festival venue 1,500 years earlier. 241 athletes from 14 nations competed in 43 events over nine days. An amateur Greek water-carrier named Spiridon Louis won the marathon, run along the road from the town to the stadium, and became an instant national hero. A 27-year-old French baron had championed the revival for nearly a decade before the games.
events.revealBlurb: April 6, 1896 — the baron was Pierre de Coubertin. Louis won his race in 2:58:50 carrying a bouquet from his village; his prize included a year's worth of free meals and a plot of land. There were no women athletes; Coubertin considered female participation "impractical, uninteresting, and incorrect."

events.title: First World Series
events.blurb: A best-of-nine championship series between the American League and National League pennant winners was played — the first time the two major leagues had agreed to a postseason championship after years of cold war. An underdog American League team, the Boston Americans, defeated the heavily favoured Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The Pirates' owner, Barney Dreyfuss, had proposed the series himself.
events.revealBlurb: October 1-13, 1903 — Boston Americans (later the Red Sox) beat the Pittsburgh Pirates. Cy Young, Boston's 36-year-old ace, started game 3 but was the losing pitcher. Dreyfuss gave his losing Pirates a share of the winners' purse to compensate. No World Series was held in 1904; it became annual from 1905.

events.title: India Wins Cricket World Cup
events.blurb: The Indian men's cricket team won their second-ever Cricket World Cup, beating Sri Lanka by six wickets in the final at a Mumbai stadium in front of a home crowd that included the country's most beloved cricketer, who was playing in his sixth and final World Cup. The tournament winner's 36-year-old captain carried the little master on his shoulders around the stadium in celebration. It was the first time any nation had won a World Cup final on its own soil.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 2011 — India beat Sri Lanka at Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai. Captain MS Dhoni hit the winning six. Sachin Tendulkar's 28 runs in his final-ever ODI innings on the way to the trophy saw him carried on teammates' shoulders around the stadium.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Battleship Potemkin Released
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Soviet director released a 75-minute silent film dramatizing a 1905 mutiny on a Russian imperial battleship. Its centerpiece, a massacre sequence on a flight of stone stairs in the Black Sea port city of Odessa, introduced a style of rapid associative editing that reshaped 20th-century cinema. A baby's pram bounces downward through the gunfire in a shot that has been quoted by dozens of later filmmakers.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 1925 — Sergei Eisenstein. The Odessa Steps massacre is fictional; no such event occurred in 1905. The pram shot has been homaged in The Untouchables, Brazil, and The Simpsons. Joseph Goebbels reportedly called the film "a marvelous film without equal."

events.title: Seven Samurai Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 207-minute epic about a defenseless farming village that hires seven masterless samurai to protect it from annual bandit raids. The film's action-adventure template — a diverse team of skilled specialists assembled for a dangerous mission — has been imitated in countless subsequent movies across every genre. One of its rainy climactic battles required 18 weeks of shooting and 500 tons of supplemental water.
events.revealBlurb: April 26, 1954 — Akira Kurosawa, starring Toshiro Mifune. The film was remade by Hollywood six years later as "The Magnificent Seven." The 2016 Marvel film "The Avengers" has been called, by its own director, a direct descendant.

events.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey Released
events.blurb: A 39-year-old New York-born director released a 149-minute science-fiction film about human evolution, artificial intelligence, and alien contact, with minimal dialogue, a four-movement structure, and long classical-music sequences of spacecraft slowly docking to the Blue Danube. The first audience walked out in droves; reviews were mixed. Within two years, it was the highest-grossing film of its year and had reshaped what cinema was permitted to do.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1968 — Stanley Kubrick. Co-written with Arthur C. Clarke. The jump cut from a primeval bone thrown into the air to a spaceship in orbit covers 4 million years in one frame. HAL 9000's voice was performed by Canadian Shakespearean actor Douglas Rain.

events.title: The Matrix Released
events.blurb: Two siblings who had directed only one feature between them released a 136-minute science-fiction film in which the world turns out to be a computer simulation and humanity is harvested by machines as a power source. The film's "bullet time" effect — a camera arcing around a frozen-mid-action character while the world resumed behind it — became an instantly iconic technique. Its cyberpunk philosophy, couture, and green-tinted aesthetic defined the turn of the millennium.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1999 — Lana and Lilly Wachowski, starring Keanu Reeves. "Bullet time" was achieved with a ring of 120 still cameras. The concept of a simulated reality — the "red pill / blue pill" — has since migrated into every internet conspiracy subculture.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.
